headline: The Race at 4-Plus Knots: Bass Committing Hard on the New-Moon Push
subhead: Valiant Rock and Plum Gut are seeing the first real fall commitment from stripers, with albies and bonito starting to push west toward the Sluiceway.
body_markdown:
The Race is running better than four knots on the bigger ebbs this week, and that's the number that matters right now. The September 10 new moon put the strongest tidal push of the early fall season into this stretch of water, and every rip from Race Rock to Plum Gut has been loaded with current for the last 48 hours. That kind of velocity doesn't just move water — it pins bunker against structure, and right now bunker are getting squeezed tight against the beaches, the inlet mouths, and the rock piles from Fishers Island Sound down through the Gut. Stripers are answering. Not picking at stragglers — committing.

The thermal picture explains where to spend your time. Kings Point is reading 70.9 on the western end of the Sound, New London's sitting at 69.4, and that gradient matters because the cooler eastern water is exactly where bass want to be once the sun gets up. Warmer western water pushes fish east looking for comfort, and the Race/Plum Gut corridor is the funnel they have to run through to get there. Combine that with new-moon current and you've got the best setup this zone has seen since spring.

Slack at Valiant Rock has been hitting right around mid-morning on the last few days' schedule, and that 20-to-25-minute window before the tide fully reverses is when the wire line bite has been most consistent. Boats working the rock in 35 to 55 feet are dropping bunker spoons and tube-and-worm on wire, letting it settle to the structure edge, then working it back with the current instead of against it. Bucktails — the 2- to 3-ounce white and chartreuse — are doing work on the up-current side of Race Rock itself when the tide's still building, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right off bottom where the rock drops into the channel. Fish being reported are mixed slot-to-overslot, with the better ones coming right at the top of the tide when current speed peaks and bait gets pinned hardest.

We flagged this pattern last week — said bass were shifting into classic early-fall staging with bunker tightening under the building moon, and that's exactly what's playing out now from Raritan Bay up through Fishers Island Sound. This is the first real feeding window of the fall run, not scattered activity, and the next few tide cycles should keep building on it as bait continues squeezing tighter.

Bluefish are backing that pattern up hard. Montauk just kicked out an 18.49-pound blue that took a $25,000 derby prize, which tells you the cooling surface water and bait concentration at the Point are about as good as they get right now. That kind of adult bluefish presence tends to spread west along the same current lines that feed the Race, and snapper blues are already thick in the back bays from here through Long Island — a reliable sign bigger blues will keep showing up tighter to structure at Plum Gut and the Sluiceway over the next week. Anyone throwing bucktails at Valiant Rock right now should expect the occasional blue to cut a bass off mid-fight; it's been happening enough that leader material is worth upgrading if you're not already running 40-pound fluoro.

The albie and bonito story is the one to watch closest. The run has gone from a tentative tease to a stabilized, genuine bite across Block Island, the Rhode Island south shore, Buzzards Bay, and Fishers Island Sound, riding a warm-water edge that's concentrating bait tight against structure. We called this exact move last week — said warmer water pushing in from the south would bring a tuna/bonito mix within range of eastern Sound boats, and that's precisely what's happening now as the pattern extends west. Plum Gut and the Sluiceway are the logical next stops. Epoxy jigs in the small 1- to 2-ounce profiles, cast into visible surface activity and worked with a fast, erratic retrieve, are the move once these fish show. It hasn't fully arrived at the Gut yet as of this week, but the trajectory says give it days, not weeks.

Fluke are a secondary story here right now — the better fish have largely staged toward deeper, cooler structure ahead of the fall exit, and what's left inshore in the Gut and Sluiceway skews small. Sea bass are improving modestly on structure spots as surface temps ease, worth a drop if you're anchored up waiting on a slack window anyway, but nobody's running out here specifically for bottom fish this week.

Looking ahead: the moon is moving off new phase over the next 72 hours, which will start easing tidal energy back down from this week's peak. That's not bad news — if anything, slightly reduced current can make presentations easier to control at Race Rock and Valiant Rock without sacrificing much bite quality, since the underlying bunker migration isn't going anywhere. The window worth prioritizing is the two days right around the next moderate tide series, fishing the last hour of ebb into slack at Valiant Rock with wire and bucktails, then watching the Gut and Sluiceway for the first real albie showing as that warm edge keeps pushing west. If you can only get out once, make it a morning tide with a hard current and clean water — that's where this bite has lived all week.
